content:
A reasonable Diwali budget for a salaried Indian household sits somewhere between one and one and a half months of take-home pay, covering clothes, gifts, puja supplies, home decoration, travel, and food across the full Navratri-to-Diwali season. Most families hit this range without specifically planning to. The issue is that very few start with a complete category list.

Key Takeaways

  • Navratri starts October 11 and Diwali falls on November 8 this year, four weeks of compounding spending pressure.
  • Average Indian millennial festive spend in 2025 was ₹32,000; Gen Z budgeted ₹25,000 but spent 47% more than planned.
  • BNPL and consumer EMI plans carry effective annual rates of 18 to 24% once the interest-free window closes.
  • A practical cap: total festive spend at 4 to 6% of annual take-home; that's ₹32,000 to ₹48,000 at ₹8 lakh income.
  • Set a total gift budget and a per-person cap before October. The gift category breaks more festive budgets than any other.

What Does a Realistic Diwali Budget Actually Look Like?

For most working Indians, a realistic Diwali budget runs between ₹25,000 and ₹60,000 for the full festive season. At 4 to 6% of annual take-home, that's ₹32,000 to ₹48,000 for someone earning ₹8 lakh after tax. Not extravagant. Specific.

The total isn't where budgets fail. The category list is. You sit down and write clothes, gifts, puja supplies, and one family dinner. You don't write the office Diwali collection you'll chip in for, the last-minute sweet boxes for neighbours, the fare hike because you booked a week before the holiday, or the child's outfit that stopped fitting by September. Those additions don't feel like budget decisions when they happen. The categories that recieve the least planning attention tend to cause the biggest overruns.

Indians spent ₹6.05 lakh crore across the festive season in 2025, the highest festive turnover India has recorded. At the household level, millennials averaged ₹32,000 and Gen Z averaged ₹25,000 but reliably spent 47% more than planned. That gap isn't carelessness. It's an incomplete category list from the start.

Should You Use EMIs or BNPL for Diwali Shopping?

Only if you're confident you'll pay the full balance before the interest-free window closes, and you've actually checked when that window ends. Used as a cash-flow tool, a 0% EMI makes real sense. Used as a substitute for money you don't have, it gets expensive fast.

Most BNPL offers during Diwali sales run 0% for three to six months. That's a reasonable deal when the cash is already in your account and you're deferring the debit for convenience or card rewards. What goes wrong is using BNPL because you genuinely can't pay now and are counting on November income to sort it out. Consumer finance plans typically run 18 to 24% per year once interest applies.

Put actual numbers on it: ₹15,000 on a six-month plan, missed by two months, costs roughly ₹1,000 extra at a 21% annual rate. Not alarming on its own. But if tight November cash also means skipping a ₹5,000 SIP instalment, the real long-term cost is closer to ₹8,000 to ₹10,000 in forgone wealth over a decade at 12% equity returns. The fee is small. The compounding tail isn't.

How Do You Set the Budget Before October 11?

Before Navratri begins, write three things: your total festive budget in rupees, a list of everyone you plan to gift with a rupee cap per person, and the one category you underestimated most in the previous year. Most budgets fall apart before they're tested because that third item is missing.

The per-person gift cap is the highest-leverage decision in the exercise. Most people lose the gift budget not by raising what they spend per person but by adding names as the season progresses. You start with eight people and a ₹600 cap. A relative's engagement happens in October. Building staff expect something. More names appear. By Diwali you're at 22 people. At ₹600 per person, that's ₹13,200 just in gifts, before anything for close family.

Setting a seperate total gift budget, not only a per-person limit, is what keeps the category honest. Decide the total first. Divide by the expected number of people. That becomes the per-person cap. If the list grows beyond the total, something else comes off. Simple and unambiguous.

A benchmark used by Indian financial planners: total festive spending at 4% to 8% of annual take-home. At ₹10 lakh after tax, that's ₹40,000 to ₹80,000 for the full season. Most practitioners suggest 5 to 6%, which is ₹50,000 to ₹60,000 at that income level. Below ₹8 lakh annual take-home, focus on the ceiling: aim for 4% or below.

One more anchor: don't let festive spending require skipping more than one SIP payment. That's the clearest signal that the celebration has crossed from a financial decision into a long-term trade-off.

The Categories That Quietly Exceed Every Estimate

Clothes tend to stay in range. Travel, gifts, and context spending rarely do.

Context spending is the box of sweets you grab because you're heading to someone's home and you definately don't want to arrive empty-handed. Not a problem once. But it happens five or six times across the season, at ₹600 to ₹800 per box, and that's ₹3,000 to ₹4,800 that appeared nowhere in the plan.

Travel is the other major one. Booking train or flight tickets within a week of a festive date typically costs 25 to 40% more than booking three to four weeks out. If your plan involves travelling to family and you haven't booked yet, that cost is already above your estimate and rises daily.

Firecrackers, for those who buy them, run ₹800 to ₹4,000 per household in Indian metros. Small line item, but most families leave it vague until they're standing at a stall in October. Put it in the plan now.

This post is for general information only, not personalized financial advice. How much you should spend depends on your income, obligations, and financial goals. These numbers are benchmarks, not prescriptions.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much do Indians typically spend on Diwali?

Average festive spending for Indian millennials runs around ₹32,000 for the Navratri-to-Diwali season. Gen Z households budget closer to ₹25,000 but regularly overshoot by around 47%. Upper-middle-income families in metros often spend ₹60,000 to ₹1.2 lakh when travel and home renovation are included.

Is it okay to buy Diwali gifts on a credit card?

Yes, if you clear the full bill before interest applies. A credit card with cashback on festive purchases is sensible. Carrying a revolving balance after the billing cycle, or using BNPL without a clear payoff plan, is where the cost becomes significant quickly.

How much should I budget per person for Diwali gifts?

For close family, ₹500 to ₹2,000 per person is a comfortable range for middle-income households. For colleagues and acquaintances, ₹200 to ₹500. The more important discipline is setting a total gift budget before the season opens, not only a per-person limit.

Can festive spending hurt my SIP investments?

Directly, if tight November cash leads to a skipped instalment. Indirectly, if you fund festive shopping with a personal loan or revolving credit at 11 to 24% annually. Skipping even one ₹5,000 SIP can cost ₹8,000 to ₹10,000 in long-term wealth over ten years at 12% equity returns.

Should I do festive shopping during Diwali sales?

Sale discounts during Navratri and Diwali are real, typically 10 to 40% off on electronics, clothing, and appliances. Build your list before the sale opens. Browsing a live sale without a prior list is how unplanned purchases enter the budget and effective discounts disappear against added items.

Is it okay to spend less on Diwali to protect savings?

Yes. Cutting on crackers, decorations, and social-obligation gifts is reasonable and often feels better in retrospect. A planned ₹20,000 Diwali is better for your finances than an unplanned ₹50,000 one. Most people find the season feels cleaner with a shorter, focused list.

The Short Version

A reasonable Diwali 2026 budget is 4 to 6% of annual take-home: roughly ₹32,000 to ₹48,000 for most salaried Indians. Set a total gift budget and a per-person cap before October 11. Use credit only where you'll clear the balance in full. If the plan requires skipping the November SIP, revise the plan before the season begins.
